research_question: What is the effect of cranberry products compared with placebo or non-active control on the occurrence of symptomatic, culture-verified urinary tract infection in women with recurrent UTIs?
outcome_description: Number of participants with at least one symptomatic, culture-verified UTI during study follow-up out of the total number of participants analyzed in each arm
positive_direction: A positive effect size (or RR < 1) indicates a lower risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTI, favoring the cranberry group over the control group
search_queries: cranberry recurrent urinary tract infection randomized trial
cranberry juice capsules placebo UTI women trial
cranberry prevention recurrent cystitis controlled trial
inclusion_criteria: Randomized controlled trials comparing any cranberry product (juice, capsules, tablets, or powder) with placebo, no treatment, or non-active control
Female participants with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections
Reporting quantitative occurrence of symptomatic, culture-verified UTI (number of participants with at least one episode) during study follow-up
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical randomized controlled trial (e.g. systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies, editorials, letters, or animal/in vitro studies)
No comparison between cranberry and a placebo, no-treatment, or non-active control arm (e.g. active-comparator trials like cranberry versus antibiotics or probiotics without an inactive control)
Studies conducted in ineligible populations (e.g. children, pregnant women, institutionalized elderly, or individuals with neurogenic bladder or urinary catheters)

Lack of quantitative data on the number of participants experiencing symptomatic, culture-verified UTI (or studies reporting only asymptomatic bacteriuria, symptoms without culture, laboratory bacterial counts, or non-clinical outcomes)
moderators_to_extract: Daily dose of proanthocyanidins (PAC) or active cranberry extract
effect_size_note: Pooled as a risk ratio (RR) with a random-effects model. Multi-arm trials with multiple cranberry arms are combined into one cranberry group. Intention-to-treat data preferred over per-protocol data. Longest follow-up on treatment used when multiple timepoints are reported.
